catalog_citation: San Roque, Lila. 2008. An introduction to Duna grammar. PhD thesis, Australian National University. xxiii+505 pp. (open access, ANU Open Research; saved, 526-page ABBYY scan with)
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.2.1 p. 55 (incl. footnote on Giles MSb) and §2.2.2.1-2.2.2.2 p. 56; §2.2.3 pp. 66-68; §2.3 p. 68
catalog_quote: Lexical roots in Duna are realised with contrastive pitch contours, and the language exhibits a word tone system in that "the word as a whole is more important than the syllable as a domain for the assignment of tones" (Donohue 1997:360). Contrastive tone melodies are contracted or stretched to fit as many syllables as there are in the word. My understanding of Duna tone is preliminary and I have not achieved a coherent analysis of Duna tone as a linguistic system (or indeed as a part of a group of inter-related prosodic systems). This description is largely limited to outlining the fundamental frequency (F0) signatures of four distinct pitch contours as they occur on monomorphemic (non-verb) roots of up to three syllables, in citation form (§2.2.2). [pp. 55-56] ... I describe monomorphemic lexical roots in Duna as being realised with one of four pitch contours: fall (F), rise (R), convex (C), or level (LV). [p. 56] ... [fn., p. 55] Giles (MSb) describes the tone system of Duna as follows: "Duna is a tone language. Depending on whether a word is uttered in a rising, falling, or level tone its meaning is altered. It appears that syllables may have a mid, high, level, rising, or falling tone". Whilst she clearly suggests in the second sentence that the domain of contrastive tone is the word, she does not comment on how this relates to the five proposed syllable tones. ... [p. 68] Contrastive pitch is not represented.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Duna is described as a word-tone language: every monomorphemic (non-verb) root carries one lexically specified pitch contour (fall, rise, convex or level; probably three underlying melodies H, LH, HL) that stretches over the whole word whatever its syllable count. The grammar contains no statement about word stress at all, neither a stress rule nor an explicit denial of stress; the only word-level prosodic contrast described is tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Rise vs convex not contrastive on monosyllables; fall vs convex not contrastive on polysyllables (p. 67), so contrast is at most three-way. Verbs and polymorphemic words are not analysed; some consonantal/wa-class verb pairs are distinguished by pitch only (sa- 'take' level vs sa- 'strike' rising, p. 82). Giles (MS) quoted in fn. on p. 55: 'Duna is a tone language.. syllables may have a mid, high, level, rising, or falling tone'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (word tone) on monomorphemic non-verb roots of up to three syllables, elicited in citation form / isolation; F0 traces from Praat. Data are Lake Kopiago (north-western) Duna.
new_statements.identity_note: San Roque 2008 describes Duna as spoken in the Lake Kopiago area (north-western dialect); the older Giles materials describe the south-eastern (Kelabo/Koroba) variety, which San Roque says differs only slightly. duna1248 is the language-level code; Glottolog gives no separate dialect codes. Note that six of the eleven Glottolog 'descriptive' references for duna1248 (Edwards 2002, Darcy et al. 2009, Elman & McClelland 1988, Kong et al. 2017, Edwards 2014, Bastiaanse 2011) are aphasia/psycholinguistics papers mis-assigned to Duna and are not about this language.

new_statements.relation_note: Secondhand: rests entirely on San Roque 2008, the same source as the catalog's existing statement, and agrees with it (Duna has word tone; no stress placement is stated). Adds nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cahill's survey classes Duna, on the strength of San Roque 2008, as a probable word-tone language (tone melodies assigned to the word as a domain), possibly of a type differing from the PNG word-tone systems he describes. He says nothing about word stress in Duna; the paper's general discussion of stress and pitch accent (pp. 1-3, 5-8) concerns other languages (Yimas, Korafe, Tinputz, Fore, etc.), not Duna. Duna is mentioned in exactly one sentence plus the reference entry.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the classification is hedged ('probable', 'possibly a different type')
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Duna (Yuna) [duc] of Southern Highlands Province, PNG; no dialect is singled out. The OPD sheet is a compilation from SIL Ukarumpa manuscripts (Cochrane & Cochrane 1963, Healey 1965/1967, Rule 1966), and Cahill's one sentence on Duna is drawn entirely from San Roque 2008.

sources.note: Chapter 2 (Phonology) never mentions stress or accent; the only suprasegmental treated is contrastive word-level pitch: §2.2 'Contrastive lexical pitch on monomorphemic words' (pp. 55-68) describes Duna as a word-tone language with four citation pitch contours (fall, rise, convex, level), possibly three underlying melodies (H, LH, HL), on non-verb roots of up to three syllables in citation form; the author calls her tone analysis preliminary. A a full-text search for stress/accent/'accent' finds only non-phonological uses.
